title: Iterative deepening versus breadth-first and depth-first search
stem: Which statement about iterative deepening search (IDS) is correct in the standard tree-search comparison?
options: The time complexity order of IDS is greater than that of BFS because IDS repeats its iterations.
The time complexity order of IDS is greater than that of DFS because IDS repeats its iterations.
The memory complexity order of IDS is like BFS, but unlike BFS, IDS is complete.
The memory complexity order of IDS is like DFS, but unlike DFS, IDS is complete.
solution: Option 4 is the intended answer under the classical tree-search assumptions: finite branching, a goal at finite depth, and ordinary DFS without a mechanism that forces it to leave an infinite branch. IDS exhausts each finite depth limit and eventually reaches the shallowest goal depth. Its live depth-first frontier is linear in the depth bound for fixed branching factor, like DFS, whereas BFS stores an exponential-width frontier. Option 1 confuses repeated work with a larger asymptotic order: for fixed branching factor greater than one, exhaustive IDS and BFS both take exponential time in the shallowest goal depth, with a constant limiting overhead ratio. Option 2 is not a general comparison because DFS depends on its maximum reached depth and branch order. Option 3 also incorrectly suggests that standard BFS is incomplete. The qualification matters: DFS with global discovery on a finite graph is complete too; this examination item is not claiming the contrary.
